enumeration.method: Independent inspection of bold SFBX1095 Theorem headings on pages 1-29 finds exactly Theorems 1 and 2. The plain-font line beginning Theorem 2 on page 24 is an explanatory reference. References end on page 29; the Appendix heading on page 30 marks the excluded boundary.

checks: The pinned title, four authors, arXiv v4 date stamp, 48-page count and source hash match the inspected PDF. Fresh extraction of pages 1-29 matches every cached evidence text.
Theorem inventory and final census pass structural validation; the inventory review hash matches, and every original claim field survives unchanged.

Both complete theorem statements were checked visually on pages 5 and 24, including all four lower-bound model conditions, A-C and numbered upper-bound conditions, exact strict elbow threshold, both tuning branches and both rates.

The observed-data model, propensity and regressions, CATE, strict Hölder floor and derivative convention were checked on pages 2 and 4. Causal identifying assumptions remain separate from the statistical regression contrast.

Definition 2 was checked on pages 15-16: local kernel, shifted Legendre coefficients, total-degree dimension q, correction basis b_hk, independently trained nuisances, estimated Gram integral, all four correction functions and both empirical/U-statistic aggregates.
The Q-hat correction preserves rho_h(X_1)^T, despite the X_2 argument in the separate main-text bias formula. The treatment first-order correction remains raw A times its residual.

The population weighted projection Q/R, transformed local measure, approximation property (6), and coordinate projection defining the population Omega convention were checked on pages 16,18-20. No normalization factor, integration-domain change or estimated nuisance requirement was added to the population projection.

Independent graph traversal confirms that the lower-bound theorem reaches only the observed model, conditional functions, CATE and Hölder class. All estimator, basis, nuisance, transformed-measure and projection requirements belong to the upper bound.

The theorem’s density-ratio sup-norm wording and ambiguous maximum grouping are preserved. The source’s expectation bound is not replaced by a high-probability claim, and its fixed-factor comparison is not changed to little-o.
All 14 direct uses and 16 related connections have source-backed explanations and matching highlight selectors. Natural-language titles use exact source keywords and original source kinds.

Ten auxiliary passages and twenty-three source-convention notes retain norms, ordered-pair normalization, nuisance-estimator caveats, smoothness-ordering prose, the correction mismatch and attainability limits. All math fragments have balanced braces.
No appendix mathematics is used. The marginal-regression alternative in Appendix A and sufficient submodel conditions in Appendix B remain outside this main-text census.

source_notes: The audited source is arXiv:2203.00837v4 dated 23 December 2023. Equality to the final journal wording has not been established.
The lower bound concerns a broader model than the upper-bound guarantee. The two are not reported as a uniform matching result under only the lower-bound assumptions.

The Q-hat polynomial argument, transformed-measure normalization, Euclidean-ball versus cube domain, density-ratio lower-bound wording and maximum grouping remain unresolved source conventions; quotations are not repaired.

Omega’s population Gram interpretation follows the main-text projection formula; a standalone printed Gram definition and a fully specified nuisance-estimation implementation are not supplied in the inspected text.

unresolved_source_references.description: The strict floor in the Hölder definition is the largest integer strictly smaller than s, so at an integer s it equals s-1. This convention also fixes the degree and dimension of the Legendre basis; the usual floor at integers is not substituted.

The lower-bound model bounds the covariate density only from above. It does not explicitly require positivity near x_0 or treatment overlap. Conditional regression versions can then be unidentified at some points. Theorem 2 adds overlap and matrix conditions; these are not transferred to Theorem 1.

The text calls gamma necessarily at least beta and later repeats gamma>=beta, but the two theorem statements do not separately list this ordering. The displayed lower-bound model constrains mu_0 and tau independently. The intended regime in the prose is recorded without inventing an extra original hypothesis.

The vector norm is defined as Euclidean, so the kernel and localized-basis indicators select a ball. Later prose describes stretching a cube, and the estimated Gram integral explicitly runs over [0,1]^d. A later convention restricts v integrals to a Euclidean ball inside that cube. These differing domains are retained, not silently reconciled by using a sup norm.

F-star is written dF(x_0+h(v-1/2)) and called a local distribution, with no explicit normalization. For an ordinary bounded density, the literal restricted pushforward has mass of order h^d, while the change-of-variable formulas with K_h and the assumed eigenvalue scales suggest a rescaled interpretation. No missing h^-d factor or conditional-probability normalization is inserted.

Definition 2’s Q-hat U-statistic term ends in rho_h(X_1)^T, but equation (9) in the bias calculation uses rho_h(X_2)^T. These are different kernels. The definition and theorem reference retain the printed estimator; the discrepancy is documented separately.

The first-order treatment correction is A(A-pi-hat), not (A-pi-hat)^2. The first-order outcome correction uses the control regression mu_0, not the marginal regression eta. Familiar R-learner formulas are not substituted for these specific source formulas.

The main text displays Omega-hat explicitly and uses Omega in the coordinate formula for the F-star-weighted linear projection. It does not separately display Omega=integral bb^T dF-star. Identifying Omega as the population Gram matrix is a source-backed interpretation of that projection formula, not a verbatim extra definition.

The norm of dF-hat-star/dF-star is said to be bounded above and below away from zero. A lower bound on this sup norm does not imply a pointwise lower bound on the density ratio. The theorem’s literal condition is retained, without strengthening it to mutual domination.

Condition 1 and equation (15) print 1+d/(2gamma)+d/(4s) vee (1+d/(2gamma)) without parentheses identifying the two arguments of the maximum. Interpreting only d/(4s) versus 1+d/(2gamma) as the maximum makes the expression agree with the piecewise rates; taking the entire preceding sum as one operand does not. Both the ambiguous formula and the unambiguous piecewise conclusion are preserved.

Condition 1 divides by the product of nuisance-error norms, which can be zero. No zero-denominator convention is given. The product remainder in Remark 11 supplies an interpretation but is not substituted for the theorem’s original fraction.

Condition 1 uses a fixed-factor less-than comparison. Remark 11 describes the third-order remainder as smaller order, which is stronger if read as little-o. The comparison symbols retain their explicit Section 2 meanings.

The nuisance estimators are trained on D^n independently of the sample used by U_n, and the empirical and U-statistic terms use the common evaluation sample. The source gives no cross-fitting or ensemble averaging rule and does not state a separate training-size asymptotic. No such procedure is added.

Remark 8 expressly says that an ordinary empirical covariate distribution need not make Omega-hat invertible at the chosen k. The high-level theorem does not construct nuisance estimators satisfying every condition. The census records its required inputs, rather than claiming an unconditional ready-to-run estimator.

The estimator uses inverse Q-hat and inverse Omega-hat with no finite-sample singularity fallback. Condition C contains an inverse-error bound, implicitly requiring that inverse to exist; density-ratio norm bounds alone do not specify an estimator regularization rule.

Theorem 2 states boundedness conditions on random nuisance quantities without explicitly saying whether they hold surely, with high probability, or conditionally. Its conclusion is an expectation bound. No high-probability-only condition or unmentioned tail/uniform-integrability condition is supplied.

F-star norm expressions in the theorem use unstarred nuisance functions, whereas the main-text calculation defines stretched versions g-star(v)=g(x_0+h(v-1/2)). This suppressed composition and the h-dependent measure must be kept visible for subsequent formalization.

The polynomial basis has total-degree dimension choose(d+strict-floor(gamma),strict-floor(gamma)), not the full tensor-product dimension (strict-floor(gamma)+1)^d. The correction basis has a separate increasing dimension k. The two bases and their population matrices are not merged.

The tuning notation tilde is defined as proportionality, while k is a basis dimension and must be an integer. The source does not specify integer rounding. The strict low-smoothness branch and otherwise branch include the elbow equality exactly as printed.

The lower bound has an infimum over estimators and supremum over the broad model. The upper bound lacks that supremum and adds distribution-estimation and regularity assumptions. Remark 2 explicitly limits matching to a more restricted submodel whose appendix details are excluded.

The observed regression contrast is defined without counterfactual variables. Consistency, positivity and no unmeasured confounding identify it as a causal effect in the introduction; these are not all automatically statistical prerequisites of the lower bound.

Remark 1 discusses replacing control-regression smoothness by marginal-regression smoothness and changing s to min(alpha,s), but the actual results for that model are in Appendix A. This alternative model is not substituted into the two inventoried main-text Theorems.

Theorem 2’s reference to condition (6) is the displayed Hölder approximation property, not Proposition 6. Main-text propositions used in the proof are not additional inventoried Theorems or automatically imported assumptions. Remark 10 repeatedly calls A-C Condition 2, and Proposition 6 refers to its own assumptions; these reference defects do not change the theorem’s explicit list.

ambient_resolution.shared: The source uses blackboard P for the true observed-data law and generic P when indexing models. X lies in [0,1]^d, A is binary, and the statistical target is tau=mu_1-mu_0 at an interior x_0. Smoothness orders are positive in the usual Hölder interpretation, radii are fixed independently of n, and the strict-floor convention is explicit. A1 resolves norms and comparison symbols, A2 empirical/U-statistic normalizations, A3 the optional causal interpretation, and A9 the average smoothness abbreviation.
ambient_resolution.1: D1 supplies iid sampling and the covariate density f. D2 supplies the propensity and treatment-specific regressions, D3 the pointwise target and mean absolute error, and D4 the exact smoothness class. The statement itself defines the model, s=(alpha+beta)/2, both rate branches and the sufficiently-large-n qualifier. It does not require the proposed estimator, independently trained nuisance inputs, approximation basis, positivity or the upper-bound density-estimation conditions. Its generic estimator is any measurable sample-based estimator of the pointwise target; no appendix lower-bound construction is required for the statement.
ambient_resolution.2: D5 supplies K_h, the strict-floor Legendre degree, total-degree dimension q and affine localization; D6 supplies the separate k-dimensional correction basis. D7 gives the independently trained nuisance estimates and Omega-hat, and D8 the full estimator with all four correction functions and both empirical terms. D9 supplies population Q and R. D10 supplies F-star, D11 the population projection and implicit Gram matrix Omega, and D12 the explicitly referenced approximation property (6). The theorem itself gives all A-C and numbered regularity conditions, both tuning regimes and the two rates. The average s is A9; the norms and ordered-pair average are A1-A2. The density ratio presupposes absolute continuity, but the source’s lower bound on its sup norm is not strengthened to pointwise domination. No proof-only proposition, appendix sufficient condition or modified estimator is inserted. Ambiguous measure normalization, maximum grouping, integration domains and the X_1/X_2 correction mismatch remain explicit source issues.
